description: We aim to tackle scientific challenges with practical solutions: working prototypes, explainable results, and demos that bring the value of NASA data to life.
summary: Errante is a public web explorer that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change using real NASA SPHEREx observations. SPHEREx surveys the entire sky in 102 infrared bands (0.75–5 µm) and revisits each spot about every six months, but its archive is built for specialists. Errante turns it into one interactive map: search any object or click any point, and Errante retrieves its real SPHEREx frames from NASA/IPAC IRSA and plays them as a dated sequence. Users can compare seasons to reveal motion, inspect light curves with uncertainties, extract SPHEREx spectra, read catalog facts with their sources, and view a 3D model built only from catalog values. We validated it on the five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis). Errante is honest by design: every panel says what SPHEREx measured, what comes from catalogs, and what is still unknown, and nothing is invented. It makes NASA's newest all-sky survey explorable for students, amateurs and scientists, with no code required.
details:
What it does

Errante is a public sky explorer built on real NASA SPHEREx data. An interactive infrared sky map (Aladin Lite with NASA/IPAC IRSA sky images) lets users search by name or coordinates, pick one of five challenge targets, or click any point in the sky. A side panel then offers four views:

- Time: the real SPHEREx exposures of that spot, played as a dated sequence (black and white per wavelength, or false-color season composites), with season comparisons that reveal motion, light curves with measurement uncertainties, and per-frame quality flags.

- Spectrum: a SPHEREx spectrum of the source from 0.75 to 5 µm, with the measured points and their limits.

- Object: catalog context (Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, AAVSO VSX, NASA Exoplanet Archive), each value with its source, plus clear "unknown, not negative" states when a service does not answer.

- 3D: a model of the star or system drawn only from catalog values and labeled "3D MODEL · NOT AN IMAGE"; planets appear only if they are confirmed in catalogs.

For any new point, Errante queries IRSA, downloads the frames, reprojects them onto a common grid, rejects bad frames, builds season coadds and false-color composites, and publishes the sequence in about one to two minutes.

How it works / tools

Python pipeline (astropy, reproject, IRSA TAP/SIA queries), a FastAPI backend with a job queue, and a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend with three.js for 3D and Aladin Lite for the sky map, deployed on a public cloud VM. We validated it on the five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Benefits and impact

SPHEREx data is open but hard to use without astronomy software. Errante lets students, teachers, amateurs and researchers see how the sky changes in a browser, with no code. Motion, variability and spectra become visible in seconds.

Creativity and factors we considered

Scientific honesty was the main design rule. Every view separates SPHEREx measurements from catalog values and model representations. Saturated cores and bad pixels are flagged, not hidden. Catalog predictions are never shown as detections, and missing data is reported as unknown instead of being invented. Edited waits in our demo video are labeled with the measured build time.

Team RetMax. AI use is declared in the repository (AI_USAGE.md): AI coding assistants helped with code, reviews and documentation; the demo narration is AI-generated (Microsoft Edge TTS); all images in the demo are screen recordings of the real app; the background music is original and was synthesized by code.

Source code (open): https://github.com/faricool54/Hackaton-NASA
